paras: The Hickory church burning was an attack in which a Black church at Hickory, Mississippi, was fired into and burned on a Monday night in late December 1881, and the town's calaboose was burned the same night. Three white men and a Black man were arrested on the charges, and a judge went to Hickory to investigate amid local alarm at the failure of officials to check lawlessness.

The only account, a short paragraph first printed in the Brandon Republican, describes "a good deal of excitement" in the Hickory community over "the lawlessness of certain parties" and the local officials' failure to suppress it. It does not say who those parties were or why the church was attacked.

On "Monday night last," according to the paragraph, shots were fired into a church described as "a negro church," and the building was then burned. The calaboose, the town's lockup, was also burned that night. The earliest printing appeared on 30 December 1881, which would put the Monday on 26 December or earlier, depending on when the Brandon Republican first ran the item. No injuries or deaths are reported, and the church is not named.

Three white men and a Black man were arrested for the attacks; none of them is named. Judge Mayers left for Hickory the day before the paragraph was written to investigate the charges against them. No report of the result of his inquiry, of an indictment or of a trial was found in the coverage.

Only two Mississippi papers are known to have carried the story, both reprinting the same Brandon Republican paragraph. The Pascagoula Democrat-Star ran it on 30 December 1881 without headline or credit, in a column of short items between jokes and a Chicago Tribune table of the year's murders. The Weekly Clarion of Jackson reprinted it on 18 January 1882 under the headline "Alleged Lawlessness Near Hickory Mississippi," with credit to the Brandon Republican. Neither paper commented, and the wording framed the attack as local disorder and weak officials rather than race, though it identified the church as Black.
